pieces.script:
When Virginia deputies raided Eliza Peake's house the day after they banned her book, they found something that terrified them more than the register itself. On October 17, 1860, one day after Henrico County ordered Eliza Peake's free Black register confiscated, Sheriff Thomas Hicks and two deputies conducted a search of her Church Hill home and documented 247 items in an official inventory filed with the county court. This was no ordinary raid — it was a calculated effort to suppress the voices of free Black Virginians who dared to challenge the status quo.

Among the seized items were 14 handwritten ledgers dating back to 1841, containing what deputies described as 'detailed genealogical records of negro families, their property holdings, and correspondence with Northern abolition societies.' These documents weren't just personal — they were a testament to the resilience of free Black communities in Virginia. The most damaging discovery was a locked tin box containing 63 letters from free Black Virginians who had successfully relocated to Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Canada between 1847 and 1860, describing routes, contacts, and resources for migration.

Henrico's Commonwealth Attorney argued the letters constituted evidence of 'advising slaves to escape' under Virginia Code Section 30, a capital offense. But no charges were filed, and all seized materials except the official register were ordered destroyed by court order on November 2, 1860. This was not just about one woman — it was about the power of knowledge in a world that sought to silence it.
